1: During property inspections, when an issue is found, a photo is taken and the matter is recorded clearly. For example, if a lampshade in the corridor is damaged, the photo can capture the scene, but the specific floor, location, and the problem found all require a lot of manual text entry so that follow-up personnel can view and handle it conveniently.
2: If this information could be organized on site, there would be no need to go back and fill in notes photo by photo; in places with poor network coverage, it is also desirable to save the record on the phone first and submit it once there is network. For inspectors, taking photos, filling in fields, and saving can be completed in one go, without switching back and forth between several screens.
3: Around this scenario, we tried using MiniCPM-V to build a mobile inspection assistant.
4: First verify the image understanding performance in the 魔搭 Notebook, then connect it to an Android phone so that the model generates observation drafts on the phone. After staff confirmation, the record is saved locally and synced to the ledger when there is network, for subsequent viewing and handling. We hope to make the record-keeping work after taking photos more convenient while preserving the opportunity for staff to check and modify.
5: 1. Turn inspection needs into a clear model task
6: The first version only handles surface phenomena that can be photographed in public areas, such as damaged lampshades, scattered objects on the floor, and visible stains on walls. It does not determine from photos whether the circuit is damaged, nor does it decide whether equipment needs to be shut down, repaired, or replaced.

A clear normal scene can be described as "no obvious surface abnormality observed," which indicates an observation within the photo range and does not mean the equipment as a whole is normal.

44: 16x and 4x are a trade-off between precision and computational cost, and a general "faster" promise cannot replace specific inspection image tests. The initial setting max_slice_nums=1 is to limit resources; small text, distant cracks, or large scenes may require increasing slices, switching to 4x, or re-shooting at close range. 45: The script saves both the raw answer and the structural validation result. Valid JSON only proves that the structure meets the requirements; whether the image is understood correctly requires manual annotation and verification. If the raw output is invalid, keep the error, allow regeneration or manual filling, and do not count invalid output as successful recognition after "fixing it up".

51: 4. Let a real phone perform image inference
52: The main path reuses the Android project of MiniCPM-V Apps. First install the official Demo, select MiniCPM-V 4.6, and download the matching language model GGUF and the vision projection file mmproj-model-f16.gguf. When the vision component is missing, the version does not match, or loading fails, the text model being able to answer questions does not mean image inference is already working.
53: This chapter prioritizes reusing, on mobile, the officially released model packages supported by that project, rather than redoing the vision conversion ourselves. Record the download source, fixed version, hashes of both files, and application commit in the deployment manifest. If the vision model is to be reconverted, the converter and projection configuration confirmed by the model team must be used, followed by re-acceptance on a real device; the single-file conversion script for the text model cannot be reused.

59: 5. From Demo to a field work interface
60: The first version of the interface can consist of three pages: "Capture, Draft Confirmation, Record List". Implement the following behaviors in order:
61: Call the camera or select an image from the album, immediately copy it to the app's private file directory and create a draft ID. Keep the original image; inference uses a JPEG copy with EXIF orientation corrected; display a preview and provide retake.
62: The user selects a location. On-site photo capture records the app's capture time; album import preserves the import source, and when the photo time is unknown, prompt personnel to verify; the import time must not be disguised as the original capture time.
63: After clicking generate, display model loading, image preprocessing, and generation status. Ensure the photo and input are saved first, then run the model; failure or interruption must not lose the captured photo.
64: Put the model object and visible phenomena into an editable form. When the JSON is invalid, fields are missing, or a retake is suggested, show the corresponding prompt and allow retaking or manual entry.
65: After the user checks the image, location, and observation and taps confirm, generate a frozen formal record, and save the record and the pending-sync status in a single local database transaction.
66: In the record list, clearly distinguish "saved on phone only", "sync succeeded", and "sync failed"; only send confirmed records when the sync button is tapped.
67: During photo processing, you can first use a long edge of 1280 pixels as a candidate, rather than handing large images to the phone without limit. Record the actual compression parameters, and use small-defect and low-light samples to check whether information is lost to compression. To prevent duplicate inference and mismatches during modification, manage button state, image hash, and draft ID together.

69: showEditableDraft and showGenerationFailure are illustrative UI events and need to be implemented according to the Activity or Fragment you use. When finalizing the complete app, build and verify it together with camera permissions, gallery selection, rotation restoration, image preprocessing, and button events.
70: When saving a formal record, the app generates a UUID, image hash, confirmer, and confirmation time, and writes the human-verified observation into InspectionRecordStore.saveConfirmed. If the two observation fields are still empty, do not enter the sync queue; if the person chooses manual entry, record their actual confirmation action. Once a formal record is confirmed, it is no longer rewritten in place; subsequent corrections are linked to the original record as a new record, to avoid sync retries submitting different content.
71: 6. Implement offline saving and online sync
72: The phone's local database stores confirmed records and the pending-sync queue, while images remain in the device's private directory. This example syncs structured observations, location, and image hash, and does not upload the original image. The hash can only be used for association and verification; the backend cannot view photos by hash. If the business needs to view photos, implement a separate user-selected attachment upload and record the sync scope.

78: Use the record ID to prevent duplicate submission
79: When syncing from the phone, do not assume that "a request timeout means the backend did not save". A common case is that the backend has already written the data and the reply is lost in transit. If the phone regenerates the ID and submits again, two identical records will appear.
80: This example uses the following conventions: the same official record always uses the same UUID; a repeated POST with the same ID and same content returns the record that already exists; the same ID with different content returns 409 Conflict. The phone marks a queue item as successfully synced only when it receives 200 or 201 and confirms that the record content in the response is the same. Timeouts, authentication failures, and conflicts all keep the item pending sync.

98: 7. Separately verify recognition performance, phone behavior, and business closed loop
99: The three types of verification answer different questions: whether the model sees correctly, whether the phone can run stably, and whether records flow reliably. Success in any one cannot replace the other two.
104: Proportion of samples whose raw output directly passes field and type validation
106: Proportion consistent with manually annotated acceptable objects, allowing predefined synonyms
108: Proportion of descriptions consistent with visible evidence in the photo, judged by annotation rules and manual review
110: Proportion of assertions about objects, causes, or handling that are not supported by the photo and input
112: Proportion of drafts requiring modification of objects or phenomena, retaining content before and after modification
114: Proportion that cannot be directly confirmed due to blur, low light, missing fields, inference interruption, etc.
115: The same image is tested separately in Notebook, the phone's original precision, or the quantized version to confirm which stage the difference comes from. EvalScope can organize custom visual question-answering data and reports; business fields and unsupported additions still require independent rules or manual review; this draft does not claim that EvalScope visual evaluation has been completed.

124: Time from cold load to being able to process images
125: v20: continuous test loading 3.916 seconds, another actual UI load 2.220 seconds. Neither run cleared the system file cache, so they cannot be regarded as storage cold starts after cache clearing. v23 loading function passes, and there is no load-time statistic under the same definition yet.
127: Latency including image preprocessing, visual encoding, and prompt processing
128: v23: A successful generation measured in one test took 7.986 seconds, including image preprocessing and reading during the generation phase. v20: 20 images averaged 13.1668 seconds, median 13.0675 seconds; this batch used pre-prepared JPEGs and did not include camera/album preprocessing.
130: From generate button to fully editable draft
131: v23: Successful generation and parsing completed in 19.927 seconds; a previous generation took 15.236 seconds and was blocked due to invalid JSON, with no crash and photos and fields preserved. v20: 20 images averaged 21.571 seconds, median 21.765 seconds, P95 27.185 seconds. These values do not include manual verification or filling time; the strict end-to-end time from button click to completed rendering of the edit screen was not measured separately.
133: Process peak memory, image dimensions, slicing and context configuration
134: v20: Peak PSS sampled per second was 2,393,000 KiB, about 2.28 GiB; RSS high-water mark was 2,513,636 KiB, about 2.40 GiB. Input was 227×227 JPEG; slice limit 1, context 8192, CPU threads 4, max 384 tokens generated, temperature 0.7, thinking disabled. v23 camera preprocessing supports downscaling the longest side to 1280, and has passed tests with 8 EXIF orientations and 48MP images; the total multi-process memory peak after remediation has not yet been re-measured.
136: 20 consecutive images, latency variation, failures, heat and battery changes
137: v20: After a single load, 20 different public cropped images were processed consecutively; 20/20 returned raw responses with no crash; 19/20 passed strict structural validation, and 1 invalid JSON was rejected. The first 5 averaged 22.862 seconds, the last 5 averaged 16.966 seconds; input content and output length differed, so thermal throttling cannot be inferred from this. Battery temperature 40→42°C, charging throughout, battery level 100%→100%, power consumption was not estimated from this. v23 has not yet re-run this batch.
139: New images generate drafts and save while offline
140: Passed. On an early real device, a newly taken photo took 17.575 seconds to generate while offline, and after confirmation entered the local queue; after network recovery, explicit sync was performed and only one record remained in the ledger. v23 additionally imported public images with airplane mode on, Wi-Fi off, and no ADB reverse network mapping, completing local generation, manual confirmation, and saving; on sync failure the record was retained, and after network recovery active sync succeeded and status refresh completed.

196: 9. Maintain the task contract when upgrading to MiniCPM-V 4.7
197: 4.7 is an optional follow-up model upgrade direction. Before upgrading, fix the specific model, official model page, language weights, vision components, conversion tools, and phone engine, rather than merely changing the model name. Use the same inspection images, the same annotations, and the same phone to re-measure effectiveness and resource costs.
198: Migration can follow this order: first single-image and structured output via Notebook, then single-image understanding and airplane-mode inference on the phone, and finally reconnect to human confirmation, the offline queue, and the ledger. Whether to adopt the 1B or 35B-A3B route is determined by target device resources and on-device measurements. Memory and speed figures from other versions, other device models, or other prompt conditions must not be written directly into this chapter.
199: The final completion criterion is: another developer can take a new photo on a supported phone, generate a draft offline, confirm it manually, and save it offline; after connecting to the network, click sync, see a unique record in the ledger, and then view the subsequent processing status. Model files, app versions, and actual phone metrics should be traceable.
